```{r message=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(p8105.datasets)
library(patchwork)

data("ny_noaa")

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  fig.width = 6,
  fig.asp = .6,
  out.width = "90%"
)

theme_set(theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "bottom"))

options(
  ggplot2.continuous.colour = "viridis",
  ggplot2.continuous.fill = "viridis"
)

scale_colour_discrete = scale_colour_viridis_d
scale_fill_discrete = scale_fill_viridis_d
```

## Problem 1 

#### Cleaning the data + basic intepretation

```{r}
ny_noaa_df =
  ny_noaa |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  separate(date, into = c("year", "month", "day"), sep = "-") |>
  mutate(
  tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10,
  tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10,
  prcp = prcp / 10
)
```

```{r}
ny_noaa_df |>
  count(snow) |>
  arrange(desc(n))
```

The most common value for snowfall was 0mm. This makes sense, as a majority of the days in a year don't typically have snow. More common values were also 25mm, 13mm, and 51mm which correspond to about an inch, half an inch, and two inches of snow. This is all logical for snowfall measurements, as they are typically measured in rounded inch counts.  

#### Plot of average temperature max

```{r}
ny_noaa_df |>
  filter(month == "01" | month == "07") |>
  group_by(id, year, month) |>
  summarize(
    mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = as.numeric(year), y = mean_tmax, group = id, color = month)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.2) +
  facet_grid(. ~ month) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Max Temperature in January vs July",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Average Max Temperature (C)"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Average maximum temperature was consistently higher in the month of July over the years. This is logical with the typical seasonality. January had more variation in max temperatures over the years in comparison to July. It seems like there are a couple of outliers: one that's about -13 degrees around January 1982 and one that's about 14 degrees around July 1988. 

#### Plots of tmax/tmin and snowfall between 0 and 100mm 

```{r}
ggp_tmax_tmin = 
  ny_noaa_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) +
  geom_hex()

ggp_snow =
  ny_noaa_df |>
  filter(snow > 0, snow < 100) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = snow, y = factor(year))) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(x = "Snowfall (mm)", y = "Year")

ggp_tmax_tmin + ggp_snow
```

## Problem 2

#### Merging and cleaning the datasets

```{r}
demo_df =
  read_csv(
    "data/nhanes_demo.csv", skip = 4, na = "NA") |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(
    sex = case_match(
      sex,
      1 ~ "male",
      2 ~ "female"),
    education = case_match(
      education,
      1 ~ "Less than high school",
      2 ~ "High school equivalent",
      3 ~ "More than high school"
    ),
    sex = factor(sex, levels = c("male", "female")),
education = factor(
  education,
  levels = c(
    "Less than high school",
    "High school equivalent",
    "More than high school"
  ))) |>
  filter(age >= 21) |>
  drop_na(sex, age, bmi, education)

accel_df =
  read_csv(
    "data/nhanes_accel.csv") |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  pivot_longer(
  min1:min1440,
  names_to = "minute",
  names_prefix = "min",
  values_to = "mims"
  ) |>
  mutate(minute = as.numeric(minute))

nhanes_df =
  left_join(demo_df, accel_df, by = "seqn")
```

#### Demographic Table

```{r}
demo_df |>
  group_by(sex, education) |>
  summarize(
    n = n()
  ) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = sex, values_from = n) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

#### Visualization of Genders vs Education

```{r}
demo_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age, fill = sex)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5) +
  facet_grid(. ~ education) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Density", fill = "Sex")
```

About half of the study group falls within the more than high school category, with the other half more relatively evenly split between the other two education groups. There are slightly less females than men in the study. For women in the more than high school education group, the age distribution peaks around 21 to 40. The groups with the less than high school education and high school equivalent generally tend to be older. 

#### Aggregation, Total Activity + Age Plot

```{r}
total_activity_df =
  nhanes_df |>
  group_by(seqn, sex, age, education) |>
  summarize(
    total_activity = sum(mims)
  )
```

```{r}
total_activity_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = total_activity, color = sex)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_grid(. ~ education) +
  labs(
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Total daily activity (MIMS)",
    color = "Sex"
  )
```

This plot makes a lot of sense -- it shows a relationship where as the age of an individual increases, their daily activity decreases. This is pretty typical as people become less mobile as they age. The less than high school education group has the steepest decline, with the highest activity levels of all education groups around age 21 and similarly low activity levels around age 80. Females with high school equivalent educations had a peak total daily activity around age 40. 

#### Time Course Education Level Plots

```{r}
nhanes_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = minute, y = mims, color = sex)) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_grid(. ~ education) +
  labs(
    x = "Time (minutes)",
    y = "Activity (MIMS)",
    color = "Sex"
  )
```

In all education levels, females generally had a slightly higher level of activity in the middle of the day. Activity reached its lowest during the night hours, which  makes sense given the fact that a majority of people are sleeping. Individuals with less than high school educations reached activity peaks at about 600 minutes into the day, with those in the other two education groups having more stable activity distributions from around 600 minutes to around 1100 minutes. 

## Problem 3

#### Merging and cleaning the data

```{r}
jan_2020_df =
  read_csv(
    "data/jan_2020_citi.csv") |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(year = 2020, month = "january")

jul_2020_df =
  read_csv(
    "data/july_2020_citi.csv") |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(year = 2020, month = "july")

jan_2024_df =
  read_csv(
    "data/jan_2024_citi.csv") |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(year = 2024, month = "january")

jul_2024_df =
  read_csv(
    "data/july_2024_citi.csv") |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(year = 2024, month = "july")

citi_df =
  bind_rows(jan_2020_df, jul_2020_df, jan_2024_df, jul_2024_df) |>
  mutate(
    month = factor(month, levels = c("january", "july")),
    weekdays = factor(
      weekdays,
      levels = c(
        "Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday",
        "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday"
      )
    )
  )
```

The resulting `citi_df` dataset has `r nrow(citi_df)` rows and `r ncol(citi_df)` columns. It has variable names: `r colnames(citi_df)`. This dataset combines data from January and July of both 2020 and 2024. Each row represents one ride, and the data overall represents 1% of rides with a total duration less than 4 hours during the listed time frames. 

#### Table for Casual vs Citi members

```{r}
citi_df |>
  group_by(year, month, member_casual) |>
  summarize(
    n = n()
  ) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = member_casual, values_from = n) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

There are a higher number of rides for members of Citi Bike versus casual users. Casual riders had a lower number of rides, which is likely the reason for them not needing memberships, so this makes sense. Additionally, there are higher rates of usage for both member types during the July months versus the January months, likely due to nicer weather in the summer. 

#### Table for 5 most popular starting locations

```{r}
citi_df |>
  filter(year == 2024, month == "july") |>
  count(start_station_name) |>
  arrange(desc(n)) |>
  head(5) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

#### Plot on days of week and ride duration

```{r}
citi_df |>
  group_by(year, month, weekdays) |>
  summarize(
    median_duration = median(duration, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = weekdays, 
    y = median_duration, 
    color = month, 
    group = month)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_grid(. ~ year) +
  labs(
    x = "Day of Week",
    y = "Median Duration",
    color = "Month"
  ) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

Median duration across both years is lower in the January month than the July month. The highest median duration for rides was on the weekends in July 2020. Generally, Saturdays during all years and months were among the highest median ride durations. 

There were relatively few electric Citi Bikes in 2020, but many more are available now. For data in 2024, make a figure that shows the impact of month, membership status, and bike type on the distribution of ride duration. Comment on your results.
